methodological_rigor.justification: The study pairs a large retrospective cohort (50,000 women from two NHSBSP centers) with a prospective arbitration reader study (22 accredited readers, 8,732 arbitration cases), with a prespecified 5% noninferiority margin, a sample-size simulation (200+ positive cases per site, 80% power), and 39-month follow-up ground truth. Statistical methods are appropriate for paired/clustered binary data (Wald's noninferiority, Obuchowski's extension of McNemar for clustered data, Holm-Bonferroni correction for the primary analysis, bootstrapped CIs for PPV/NPV, RJafroc for localization). Weaknesses include: inability to blind readers to the AI arm (acknowledged as clinically realistic), use of the same 5% noninferiority margin for sensitivity and specificity despite very different negative/positive case counts (acknowledged), unmatched reader pairs across batches, exclusion of 8.7% of cases by AI criteria that would still require human reading, and underpowered subgroup analyses (25/29 subgroups with <300 positive cases) with no multiplicity adjustment (acknowledged as exploratory).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a retrospective comparative diagnostic accuracy study with an embedded prospective arbitration reader study — best classified as an individual cohort study (Oxford 2b) given the longitudinal 39-month follow-up and comparison of two parallel reading workflows applied to the same cases. Clinical relevance is high: the question directly addresses whether AI can safely replace a second reader in the UK NHSBSP in the face of a 30–40% radiologist shortfall, with patient-relevant endpoints (sensitivity for screen-detected, interval, and next-round cancers; specificity; recall rate; CDR) and quantified workload reductions (36–44% reading-time reduction). Findings explicitly inform upcoming prospective trials (e.g., EDITH) and operating-point/vendor-tuning decisions prior to NHSBSP deployment, giving a direct and near-term translational path, though not yet practice-changing without prospective confirmation.

reporting_quality.justification: STARD applies as the primary design is a comparative diagnostic accuracy evaluation; the study reports ethics approval (East Midlands REC 22/EM/0038, BSPRAC_0093), ISRCTN registration (60839016), a Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary, prespecified primary endpoint and noninferiority margin, a Fig. 1e flow diagram, detailed index-test (AI v1.2) description with training-data composition, reference-standard definition (39-month follow-up, bounding boxes), reader characteristics, exclusion criteria, and 2x2 tables in supplementary materials. Minor STARD gaps include limited description of handling of indeterminate results beyond the stated exclusions, no explicit QUADAS-style risk-of-bias discussion, and ethnicity/IMD subgroup details reference redacted URLs. Data/code availability is partial: Source Data for all four figures is referenced, but no deposition in a named public repository for the underlying OMI-DB subset or analysis code is clearly stated in the blinded text (OMI-DB is referenced as the source but access terms are not specified here).

novelty_literature.justification: The empirical novelty is clearly articulated and credible: this is, as positioned, the first large-scale (50,000 women, two centers, two different NHSBSP arbitration protocols) study to prospectively perform arbitration with human reader pairs under both human-arm and AI-arm conditions rather than simulating arbitration computationally (refs 2, 5–7) or using small enriched datasets (ref 8, 278 cases with ultrasound). Methodological novelty includes the combination of long-term follow-up (3-year interval and next-round cancers), lesion-level localization comparison at arbitration (JAFROC FoM), and human-factor surveys (NASA-TLX, trust). Novelty is bounded by substantial adjacent prior work (MASAI, Dembrower, Lancet Digital Health retrospective studies, Frazer et al. 2024) that evaluates AI integration in screening, and the AI tool itself is a vendor update of a well-known model (McKinney 2020), so this is a strong confirmatory and extending contribution rather than a first-in-class paradigm shift.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and logically organized: the abstract is quantitatively grounded and faithful to the full text; the Methods section is detailed and well-sectioned (case selection, AI system, readers, paperwork, hanging protocol, QC, analysis, sample size); and the Discussion is explicitly structured around seven aspects which is both unusual and effective for readability. Figure captions (Figs 1–4) are informative and standalone-interpretable, including sample sizes and error-bar definitions. Minor weaknesses include some dense tables (Table 1 and Table 4 in the extracted markdown are difficult to parse as rendered, likely a formatting artefact), occasional long paragraphs in the Discussion, and some redacted URL placeholders that break reference continuity, but overall the writing is publication-ready.

key_strengths: Large (n=50,000), two-center NHSBSP cohort with 39-month longitudinal follow-up permitting assessment of interval and next-round cancers, not just screen-detected
Genuine prospective arbitration reader study with 22 accredited readers across two different real-world arbitration protocols, rather than simulated arbitration as in prior work

Prespecified noninferiority design with appropriate paired/clustered statistics (Wald, Obuchowski-McNemar, Holm-Bonferroni), sample-size simulation, and explicit treatment of subgroup analyses as exploratory and hypothesis-generating

Lesion-level localization analysis (JAFROC) and detailed investigation of the 93 positive cases where AI correctly recalled but arbitration overruled, with mechanistic insight into false-positive ROIs and prior-image effects

Direct policy relevance: workload quantification (36–44% reading-time reduction, arbitration rate increases of 22–142%), vendor-manufacturer performance differences (Siemens underperformance tied to 0.9% training representation), and explicit lessons for prospective trials
key_concerns: Inability to blind readers to AI arm (acknowledged but limits internal validity and may bias reader behavior toward or against AI prompts)
Same 5% noninferiority margin applied to specificity and sensitivity despite much larger negative-case base, acknowledged but not corrected post hoc

Many subgroups (25/29) underpowered with <300 positive cases, and no multiplicity adjustment; Siemens and 'not-specified ethnicity' signals of worse AI performance are therefore hypothesis-generating only
Data and code availability in the blinded text is limited to figure-level source data; OMI-DB access terms and analysis code deposition not clearly stated
Generalizability constrained to triennial NHSBSP screening, two London centers, predominantly Hologic imaging, and a single vendor's AI tool
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a methodologically rigorous, large-scale, policy-relevant evaluation of AI as a second reader with arbitration in a real national screening program, with clear advances over prior simulated-arbitration literature; the content is consistent with top-tier oncology/clinical-AI journals (Tier 1 range), warranting minor revisions to address blinding bias framing, data/code availability, and the asymmetric noninferiority margin.
